Electromagnetic wave

 Home Physics Branches of physics Electromagnetism
OurBigBook.com Words: 12k Articles: 129
An electromagnetic wave is a propagating disturbance of the electric field and magnetic field obeying the Maxwell equations. In source-free vacuum its speed is
c=μ0​ϵ0​​1​≃2.998×108m/s,
(1)
the speed of light. An electromagnetic wave can travel through vacuum: a conducting medium is unnecessary. A single traveling plane electromagnetic wave has mutually perpendicular electric field, magnetic field, and propagation direction. This statement applies to that wave; arbitrary near and far field configurations need not share these directions or the relation ∣B∣=∣E∣/c.
The visualization compares perpendicular components on a common scale: cB has the same units as E. The curves are field values along space, rather than paths traced by particles. Their common phase moves toward +z, while the Poynting vector records the associated energy flux.
The electromagnetic wave equation gives a propagation law, while the full Maxwell equations additionally enforce the field directions and relative amplitudes. This is why solving an independent scalar wave equation for each component is insufficient to construct an electromagnetic wave. [ref].

Root mean square magnetic field from beam power (Brms​=μ0​P/(cA)​)

Words: 44
Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
For a uniform plane-wave beam of cross section A, mean intensity is P/A=cBrms2​/μ0​. Hence Brms​=μ0​P/(cA)​. A sinusoidal peak amplitude is 2​ times the rms amplitude. A Gaussian beam requires a stated waist or diameter convention before inferring its on-axis field from total power.

Rectangular electromagnetic cavity (ν=2c​(l/Lx​)2+(m/Ly​)2+(n/Lz​)2​)

Words: 97
Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
A closed rectangular perfect conductor cavity has discrete normal modes selected by zero tangential electric field at the walls. Each frequency has the displayed form. With all three indices positive there are two independent polarizations of an electromagnetic wave; modes with exactly one zero index have one, and those with two zero indices are absent. For example the n=0 family can have Ez​∝sin(πlx/Lx​)sin(πmy/Ly​), independent of z. It satisfies the wall conditions because Ez​ is normal to the z faces and tangential to the side walls. Omitting such zero-index families is harmless for leading bulk density of states, but changes the low-temperature physics of a thin cavity.

Wave impedance (Z=μ/ϵ​)

Words: 163 Articles: 2
Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
For a plane electromagnetic wave in a homogeneous, linear, lossless, isotropic medium with permittivity ϵ and magnetic permeability μ, the wave impedance relates the field amplitudes by Z=E/H=μ/ϵ​. Its units are ohms. Impedance differences determine the normal-incidence amplitude Fresnel equations, r=(Z2​−Z1​)/(Z2​+Z1​) and t=2Z2​/(Z2​+Z1​), with a common tangential electric-field axis.

Power transmission coefficient (T=Ptransmitted​/Pincident​)

Words: 119 Articles: 1
Wave impedance OurBigBook.com
The ratio of transmitted to incident normal time-averaged power for a specified wave and interface. Converting a field-amplitude transmission coefficient into power requires the appropriate impedances or flux normalization. For a displacement wave on a string with impedance Z, T=(Z2​/Z1​)∣t∣2; using an electric-field amplitude in electromagnetic waves instead gives the corresponding electromagnetic flux ratio. Amplitude squared alone is sufficient only when the relevant incident and transmitted normalizations agree.

Transmitted power (Pt​=TPi​)

Words: 49
Power transmission coefficient OurBigBook.com
The energy flux carried into a transmitted wave, integrated over the relevant cross section. The power transmission coefficient compares this with incident power. A displacement or field-amplitude transmission coefficient must be converted with the appropriate wave impedances; its squared modulus alone need not be the power fraction. This distinction applies both to electromagnetic waves and transverse string waves.

Electromagnetic waveguide

Words: 555 Articles: 7
Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
An electromagnetic waveguide confines an electromagnetic wave across its axis while allowing it to travel along the axis. Conducting walls or changes of refractive index select transverse normal modes: reproducible cross-sectional field patterns with their own longitudinal wavenumbers. A hollow metal pipe and an optical fiber are different realizations of this principle. Their usefulness is to deliver electromagnetic energy along a chosen route instead of letting it spread freely.
For a uniform vacuum-filled conducting guide, write a normal mode's axial and time dependence as ei(βz−ωt). Here ω>0 is angular frequency, β is the longitudinal wavenumber, and k⊥2​ is the transverse eigenvalue selected by the wall boundary conditions. The electromagnetic wave equation separates into
β2=c2ω2​−k⊥2​.
(2)
The geometry consumes part of the available squared wavenumber: when ω/c<k⊥​, this branch is an evanescent wave rather than a propagating normal mode. The waveguide cutoff frequency is therefore a property of a specified branch and geometry. A transverse electromagnetic mode in a suitable two-conductor geometry can have k⊥​=0 and no positive geometric cutoff. An optical fiber needs its own dielectric boundary conditions, rather than the metal-wall formulas below.
The rectangular electromagnetic waveguide makes these ideas explicit with a single sine profile. The scalar-potential conducting waveguide modes give a broader construction. At an open aperture, a confined field can radiate into the electromagnetic aperture angular spectrum; it need not remain one guided normal mode.

Optical waveguide

Words: 36
Electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
An optical waveguide confines an optical normal mode transversely while permitting longitudinal propagation. A higher-refractive index layer between lower-index layers provides a simple dielectric realization. In a double heterostructure laser, overlap of the guided field with the carrier-rich active layer improves useful optical gain.

Transverse electric mode (Ez​=0)

Words: 41
Electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
A guided electromagnetic wave whose electric field has no component along the propagation axis. Its magnetic field can have a longitudinal component. In an empty perfectly conducting rectangular electromagnetic waveguide, transverse wave numbers determine a nonzero cutoff frequency. This differs from a transverse electromagnetic mode, in which both fields are transverse.

Planar dielectric waveguide

Words: 118 Articles: 2
Electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
A dielectric slab surrounded by lower-index material confines waves with an oscillatory core profile and evanescent exterior tails. In an isotropic, nonmagnetic symmetric slab, an even transverse-electric field has core profile cosKz and matches to exponential tails through Ktan(Kd)=K′. The transverse constants also satisfy K2+K′2=(ϵr​−1)ω2/c2 for vacuum exterior.

Fundamental even mode of a symmetric dielectric slab (utanu=w,u2+w2=V2)

Words: 69 Articles: 1
Planar dielectric waveguide OurBigBook.com
Set u=Kd, w=K′d, and V=(ωd/c)ϵr​−1​. The circle in the first quadrant falls from w=V, while utanu rises from zero to its first pole. A unique first-branch intersection exists for every V>0. It yields a nodeless even bound field. At exactly zero index contrast there is no confined mode; as contrast tends to zero from above its tail extends without bound.

Scalar-potential conducting waveguide modes (γ2=ω2/c2−k2)

Words: 64
Electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
For dependence ei(kz−ωt), a Helmholtz equation (Δ⊥​+γ2)ψ=0 generates transverse-magnetic fields e⊥​=∇⊥​ψ, ez​=−iγ2ψ/k, b⊥​=ωz×∇⊥​ψ/(kc2), bz​=0, for k=0. The conducting wall requires a Dirichlet boundary condition on ψ. A transverse-electric representation is e⊥​=z×∇⊥​ψ, ez​=0, b⊥​=−k∇⊥​ψ/ω, bz​=iγ2ψ/ω, with a Neumann boundary condition. These are families of modes, not a completeness assertion for multiply connected guides and their possible TEM fields.

Electromagnetic aperture angular spectrum (q=(κ,ν,η),κ=k2−ν2−η2​)

Words: 107
Electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
For an aperture normal to ex​, let Fy​,Fz​ be its tangential electric field traces extended by zero outside the aperture. With the outgoing branch of κ, the Weyl plane-wave representation and the curl aperture integral give a spectrum proportional to (−(νFy​+ηFz​)/κ,Fy​,Fz​). Each wave is transverse to q. The longitudinal electric component is regenerated by oblique diffraction even when it vanishes at the input. For G=eikr/(4πr) and a unit prefactor on the stated curl integral, the spectrum has an overall factor 1/2; a doubled half-space Green kernel gives factor one. The normalization must follow the chosen Green kernel and equivalent-current convention.

Rectangular electromagnetic waveguide

Words: 2k Articles: 7
Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
Take a straight hollow rectangular electromagnetic waveguide with vacuum interior 0<x<a, 0<y<b and axis z, where a>b>0. Its four walls are ideal perfect conductors. The time-dependent Maxwell equations require zero tangential electric field and zero normal oscillating magnetic field at these walls. Real metal has finite electrical conductivity, so real guides lose electromagnetic energy by Joule heating; the perfect-wall model isolates confinement and wave dispersion from that loss.
The simplest propagating transverse electric mode of a rectangular waveguide is TE10​. “Transverse electric” means Ez​=0, not that the magnetic field is also wholly transverse. With real peak scale E0​, its complex amplitudes, including the common axial factor, can be written
Ey​Bx​Bz​​=E0​sin(πx/a)eiβz,=−ωβ​E0​sin(πx/a)eiβz,=−aωiπ​E0​cos(πx/a)eiβz.​Ex​By​​=Ez​=0,=0,​
(3)
The physical fields are the real parts after multiplication by e−iωt. In particular, Ey​ is zero at x=0,a, maximal at x=a/2, and independent of y. At y=0,b it is normal to the metal, so it need not vanish there. The TE10​ electric field crosses the narrow gap, while its strength varies across the broad dimension.
For an original example choose a=30mm, b=12mm and f=1.25fc​, where fc​=c/(2a). With c=299792458m/s, this gives
fc​λ0​​=4.99654097GHz,=48mm,​fβ​=6.24567621GHz,=25πm−1,​λg​​=80mm.​
(4)
Here λ0​=c/f is vacuum wavelength and λg​=2π/β is guided wavelength. The next cutoff is TE20​ at 2fc​; TE01​ starts at (a/b)fc​=2.5fc​. Thus only TE10​ can propagate at the chosen frequency, although a source or discontinuity can additionally excite local evanescent waves. These are calculated values, not specifications or measurements of a commercial guide.

Transverse magnetic mode of a rectangular waveguide (Ez​∝sin(nπx/a)sin(mπy/b))

Words: 73
Rectangular electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
In a hollow rectangular electromagnetic waveguide with perfect conductor walls and axis z, a transverse magnetic polarization has Bz​=0 and a nonzero longitudinal electric field Ez​. The wall boundary conditions impose Ez​=0 around the transverse rectangle. Separation of variables therefore gives Ez​=E0​sin(nπx/a)sin(mπy/b)ei(kz​z−ωt), with n,m≥1. Setting either index to zero makes the entire field vanish. Thus there is no TMn0​ or TM0m​ branch. The transverse eigenvalue is k⊥2​=(nπ/a)2+(mπ/b)2, with dispersion relation ω2/c2=kz2​+k⊥2​. This exclusion is specific to this geometry and these boundary conditions.

Waveguide cutoff frequency (ωmn​=cπm2/a2+n2/b2​)

Words: 561 Articles: 1
Rectangular electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
The waveguide cutoff frequency separates oscillatory axial propagation from exponential decay for a particular normal mode. For the vacuum-filled rectangular electromagnetic waveguide, the dispersion relation is
κmn2​=(amπ​)2+(bnπ​)2,ωmn​=cκmn​,β2=c2ω2−ωmn2​​.
(5)
For a transverse electric mode of a rectangular waveguide, m,n are nonnegative integers but not both zero. For a mode with Bz​=0 and nonzero Ez​, both indices must be positive. The lowest cutoff for a>b is consequently ω10​=πc/a, or ordinary frequency fc​=c/(2a).
A square cross-section instead gives equal TE10​ and TE01​ cutoffs. The absence of a transverse electromagnetic mode is specific to this hollow pipe, rather than all electromagnetic waveguides.[ref]
For ω>ωmn​, choose real β>0 for propagation toward +z. For 0<ω<ωmn​, a field decaying into a semi-infinite guide has
β=iα,α=cωmn2​−ω2​​>0,eiβz=e−αz.
(6)
A finite section can contain both growing and decaying axial solutions set by its two ends; the single decaying solution is not a complete finite-section transmission calculation. At exact cutoff β=0, the two axial solutions become a constant and a linear function of z: there is no finite axial wavelength for a traveling sinusoid.
In the chosen a=30mm guide at f=0.8fc​=3.99723277GHz, the TE10​ branch has α=20πm−1. Its amplitude decay length is 1/α≃15.9155mm; after 50mm, its normalized wave amplitude is e−π≃0.0432139. This is geometric evanescence even with ideal walls, not Joule heating. A single decaying branch has zero cycle-averaged axial Poynting vector: substituting β=iα makes Bx​ a quarter-cycle out of phase with Ey​. Coupling across a finite section requires the complete boundary-value solution.

Waveguide phase and group velocities (vph​vg​=c2)

Words: 244
Waveguide cutoff frequency OurBigBook.com
For a propagating branch of an ideal vacuum-filled rectangular electromagnetic waveguide, the phase velocity tracks constant wave phase along the axis, whereas the group velocity describes a sufficiently narrow, weakly distorted wave packet. Using ω2=c2β2+ωc2​ gives
vph​=βω​=1−(ωc​/ω)2​c​,vg​=dβdω​=ωc2β​=c1−(ωc​/ω)2​.
(7)
Thus vph​>c, 0<vg​<c, and vph​vg​=c2. Differentiating the dispersion relation proves the second formula; dividing it by β2 proves the first. This is the same mathematical structure as Klein-Gordon packet velocities. In the stipulated f=1.25fc​ example,
vph​=35​c,vg​=53​c.
(8)
Over 0.30m, the corresponding narrow-envelope delay is (0.50m)/c, approximately 1.668ns. Timing a carrier wave crest would give 0.6004ns; it does not time the arrival of a newly introduced message.
There is an independent energy check. For the forward TE10​ fields, the average axial Poynting vector is ⟨Sz​⟩=β∣Ey​∣2/(2μ0​ω). Integrating across the guide gives average power P and average electromagnetic energy per unit length U′:
P=4μ0​ωabβE02​​,U′=4ϵ0​abE02​​,U′P​=ωc2β​=vg​.
(9)
The transverse sine and cosine squared each integrate to a/2; β2+(π/a)2=ω2/c2 then makes the integrated electric and magnetic contributions to U′ equal. The axial energy transport therefore agrees with the group velocity in this ideal model.
As ω↓ωc​, vg​→0 and vph​→∞; exactly at cutoff ω/β is undefined. Strong wave dispersion close to cutoff also limits the narrow-packet approximation. Neither a large phase velocity nor a pulse peak establishes superluminal information velocity; front velocity asks a separate causal question. In a uniform filling with constant positive permittivity ε and magnetic permeability μ, replace c by u=1/εμ​, giving vph​vg​=u2. Frequency-dependent material response or significant loss requires differentiating the actual dispersion relation, so this product is not universal.

Transverse electric mode of a rectangular waveguide (TEmn​)

Words: 233 Articles: 1
Rectangular electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
A transverse electric mode of a rectangular waveguide has Ez​=0 while its axial magnetic field is generally nonzero. For time dependence e−iωt and axial dependence eiβz, set Δ=(ω/c)2−β2. The Maxwell equations reconstruct the transverse components from Bz​:
Bx​=Δiβ​∂x​Bz​,By​=Δiβ​∂y​Bz​,Ex​=Δiω​∂y​Bz​,Ey​=−Δiω​∂x​Bz​.
(10)
The axial complex amplitude satisfies a transverse Helmholtz equation, (∂x2​+∂y2​+Δ)Bz​=0. Zero tangential electric field at each perfect conductor wall becomes a Neumann boundary condition on Bz​. Separation of variables gives
Bz​=B∗​cos(mπx/a)cos(nπy/b)eiβz,Δ=κmn2​.
(11)
The index m counts half-periods across a, and n across b. Either index can vanish, allowing TE10​; both cannot vanish. Indeed a spatially constant axial oscillating magnetic field would give nonzero changing magnetic flux through the cross-section, whereas the line integral of tangential electric field around its metal boundary is zero. The integral form of Faraday's law excludes this TE00​ candidate. Dividing the reconstruction formulas by Δ=0 would be invalid and cannot produce the separate transverse electromagnetic mode.
For m=1,n=0, choose B∗​=−i(π/a)E0​/ω. The formulas recover exactly the Ey​, Bx​ and Bz​ in rectangular electromagnetic waveguide. In particular, the transverse magnetic field accompanies Bz​ and ensures zero divergence; an oscillating longitudinal magnetic field on its own is not the guided solution.

Evanescent transverse electric mode in a rectangular waveguide (κ2=(π/a)2−ϵr​ω2/c2)

Words: 66
Transverse electric mode of a rectangular waveguide OurBigBook.com
Below the lowest waveguide cutoff frequency, the axial wave number of the TE10​ mode is iκ, with κ>0. For a real peak scale E0​ and time convention e−iωt, Ey​=E0​sin(πx/a)e−κz, Bx​=−iκEy​/ω and Bz​=−iE0​(π/a)cos(πx/a)e−κz/ω. The electric field and magnetic field are in quadrature. A single decaying mode in a lossless semi-infinite guide consequently has zero time-averaged Poynting vector, although its instantaneous field stores energy.

Guided wavelength (λg​=2π/β)

Words: 141
Rectangular electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
The guided wavelength is the distance for a 2π change of axial wave phase in a propagating normal mode. For the vacuum-filled rectangular electromagnetic waveguide,
λg​=1−(fc​/f)2​λ0​​,λg2​1​=λ02​1​−(2a)21​
(12)
for TE10​, with λ0​=c/f and f>fc​. It exceeds the vacuum wavelength at the same frequency. This longer axial spacing is consistent with vph​>c: multiplying λg​ by f gives the phase velocity, not the group velocity.
Two oppositely traveling fields at the same frequency form a standing wave. For a perfect electric short at z=0, the total electric field is proportional to sin(βz)sin(πx/a), so successive axial electric nodes are separated by
d=βπ​=2λg​​.
(13)
Thus neighboring minima in a slotted line scan give half a guided wavelength. In the original a=30mm, f=1.25fc​ example, d=40mm implies λg​=80mm, not 40mm. Combined with the chosen f, the inferred broad dimension is a=λ0​/[21−(λ0​/λg​)2​]=30mm. Below cutoff, β is imaginary and 2π/β is not a physical periodic spacing.

Slotted-line waveguide measurement

Words: 267
Rectangular electromagnetic waveguide OurBigBook.com
MIT's documented slotted-line waveguide measurement shorts one end of a rectangular electromagnetic waveguide and excites it through a probe coupled by capacitance. A second such probe moves through a longitudinal slot, aligned with the wall electric current to reduce disturbance. Its output locates axial standing wave nulls. The book's standing-wave setup chooses a frequency above the first waveguide cutoff frequency and below higher-mode cutoffs. Lowering it below the first cutoff instead reveals spatial decay away from the source. The text supplies apparatus and an observable comparison, rather than a table of measured null positions.[ref]
The inference can be checked without assuming that detector output is proportional to electric field amplitude. At fixed measured frequency, record several minima at coordinates z0​,…,zN​; then estimate λg​=2(zN​−z0​)/N when the minima are consecutive. This uses positions alone. Compare the result with the guided wavelength prediction using independently measured a and f. The 40mm spacing above is a synthetic example, not a reading from the MIT apparatus.
Additional proposed controls are to keep probe insertion fixed, repeat the scan in both directions, recheck source frequency, and compare shallow probe settings for shifts in the minima. These test probe loading, mechanical backlash and drift. A deliberately reflecting termination supplies the standing wave; varying its position should translate the pattern without changing adjacent-null spacing in a uniform single-mode region. Source-adjacent evanescent waves, unintended reflections, additional propagating normal modes, detector noise and finite positional resolution can spoil that inference. A disappearing remote signal alone does not distinguish below-cutoff decay from loss or poor excitation, and a scan at one frequency does not measure a pulse's group velocity.

Transverse magnetic polarization (H=Hy​y​)

Words: 47
Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
Relative to a propagation plane, transverse magnetic polarization has its magnetic field perpendicular to that plane. At a perfectly conducting corrugation its scalar magnetic component obeys a Neumann condition. It reduces to a scalar two-dimensional problem, but not to the Dirichlet problem for the transverse electric component.

Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
Relative to a propagation plane, transverse electric polarization has its electric field perpendicular to that plane. For a conducting corrugation independent of the perpendicular coordinate, the scalar electric component obeys the Helmholtz equation with Dirichlet data at the metal surface.

TE wave equation in a stratified magnetodielectric (Ey,xx​+Ey,zz​−μμ′​Ey,z​+ω2μεEy​=0)

Words: 44
Transverse electric polarization OurBigBook.com
With permittivity and permeability depending only on z and time dependence eiωt, a transverse electric polarization E=y​Ey​(x,z) obeys the displayed equation. Maxwell's equations give Hx​=Ey,z​/(iωμ) and Hz​=−Ey,x​/(iωμ). The latter satisfies Hz,xx​+Hz,zz​+(μ′/μ)Hz,z​+[ω2με+(logμ)′′]Hz​=0. At normal incidence Hz​=0; the nonzero magnetic component is Hx​.

Refractive index (n)

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
The refractive index compares the phase velocity of light in a medium with the vacuum speed of light c. For a transparent, uniform medium with isotropy and a positive-index propagation branch,
n(ω)=vph​(ω)c​=ωck(ω)​.
(14)
Here ω>0 is the angular frequency, k>0 is the wavenumber, and vph​=ω/k is the speed of a surface of constant wave phase. The refractive index is a dimensionless quantity; it is a property of a specified material response at a specified frequency, rather than a universal number attached to the word “glass”. Total internal reflection
Words: 1k Articles: 4
Snell law for electromagnetic waves OurBigBook.com
Total internal reflection occurs when a wave travels from higher to lower refractive index above the critical angle for total internal reflection, leaving no propagating transmitted plane electromagnetic wave normal to the interface.
At an infinite planar interface, total internal reflection returns all incident normal power in the reflected plane electromagnetic wave. Assume homogeneous dielectrics with isotropy, linearity, no dielectric loss, magnetic permeability μ0​, and positive real refractive indices n1​>n2​. Above the critical angle for total internal reflection, both TE polarization and TM polarization have unit optical reflectance despite the external evanescent wave.[ref]
This makes total internal reflection useful for guiding light in an optical fiber: suitable internal incidence angles keep energy inside successive boundaries. Its more surprising feature is that perfect optical reflectance coexists with an external electric field. The evanescent field in total internal reflection can interact with a nearby object, as the frustrated total internal reflection experiment demonstrates.
For an original idealized example, choose n1​=1.5, n2​=1 at vacuum wavelength λ0​=633nm. At angle of incidence 40∘, Snell law for electromagnetic waves gives an angle of refraction arcsin(1.5sin40∘)≈74.6186∘, so a transmitted light ray still emerges. At θc​≈41.8103∘, its direction becomes tangent to the boundary. At 50∘, the proposed sine of a real angle of refraction would be 1.5sin50∘≈1.14907>1: the transmitted wavevector must instead have an imaginary normal component. These are predictions for the stipulated media, not measured properties of a particular block.
A real semicircular-block experiment isolates this threshold. The University of Maryland laboratory instructions place a laser, motor-driven rotation stage and photodetector together; an aperture limits the detector voltage. The semicircular block is centered on the rotation axis, with the photodetector aligned along its flat face. The instructions identify a strong grazing-beam signal and a weaker signal just before the critical angle for total internal reflection. The readout is detector voltage versus stage angle. Retracing the incident laser beam identifies normal incidence for alignment.[ref]
The semicircular shape supplies a geometric control: a light ray passing radially through the curved face enters at normal incidence, avoiding additional entrance refraction. The weaker signal near the flat face locates a limiting angle of refraction; a vanishing remote-detector signal alone would not establish that the external electric field vanishes. Beam width and alignment limit angular resolution; no measured threshold or decay depth is supplied.[ref]

The critical angle for total internal reflection is the boundary between outgoing refraction and an evanescent wave, rather than an angle at which the external electric field abruptly disappears. Write n1​=n−​ and n2​=n+​. At the threshold, Snell law for electromagnetic waves has θt​=90∘, hence
θc​=arcsin(n1​n2​​),0<n2​<n1​.

Here inverse sine selects 0<θc​<90∘. For n1​=1.5 and n2​=1, sinθc​=2/3 and θc​≈41.8103149∘. The threshold is independent of polarization of an electromagnetic wave under the stated assumptions.
A short proof using phase matching at a planar wave interface reveals all three cases at once. Choose a Cartesian coordinate system with boundary z=0, incident medium z<0, and transmitted medium z>0. With vacuum wavenumber k0​=2π/λ0​, the shared tangential wavevector component is q=n1​k0​sinθ. The dispersion relation in medium two gives
k2z2​=n22​k02​−q2=k02​(n22​−n12​sin2θ).
(31)
Below θc​, choose the positive real square root for an outgoing plane electromagnetic wave. At θc​, k2z​=0: there is a grazing wave, with zero normal average power but no exponential confinement in z. Above θc​, choose k2z​=iκ with κ>0, so the wave amplitude decays into the second half-space.
If n1​≤n2​, no nongrazing angle of incidence produces this threshold. As n2​/n1​→1 from below, θc​→90∘; as that ratio tends to zero, θc​→0. These limits explain why a larger refractive index contrast permits confinement over a wider range of internal angles.

Frustrated total internal reflection

Total internal reflection OurBigBook.com
Frustrated total internal reflection occurs when a nearby second high-index dielectric couples to the evanescent field in total internal reflection, allowing power to cross a finite low-index gap. The extra boundary changes the dielectric-interface boundary conditions; the gap field need not be a single decaying evanescent wave. Consequently, the zero normal Poynting vector calculation for two infinite half-spaces does not forbid transmission in this three-medium geometry.
Harvard’s actual demonstration uses two right-angle glass prisms, a helium-neon laser, a small clamp and two perpendicular screens as detectors. The contact faces are cleaned and placed opposite each other, with the clamp protecting the corners. Increasing pressure narrows the intervening air film; the observed beam routing changes gradually from total internal reflection toward onward transmission. The broad-gap reflecting configuration supplies the comparison for the narrow-gap transmitting configuration. This is a qualitative readout: the page explicitly says the gap is not measured.[ref]
The inference is that the lower-index region can mediate electromagnetic energy transfer when another boundary is nearby. The demonstration does not determine a numerical evanescent penetration depth, resolve gap uniformity, or establish a three-layer transmission coefficient. For the constructed 50∘ example, δ≈178nm identifies the scale over which the isolated-interface field remains appreciable; substituting e−2g/δ for a gap transmission fraction would omit the changed boundary fields and their interference. A quantitative gap calculation must solve the full Maxwell equations with both boundaries.

In the radiation zone of a localized source, the leading electromagnetic fields decay as 1/R, are transverse to the observation direction, and satisfy B=R×E/c. Terms decaying faster than 1/R do not contribute to the limiting radiated power.

⟨S⟩=4πr2P​

at distance r. For monochromatic vacuum radiation, its electric-field amplitude is E0​=2⟨S⟩/(ϵ0​c)​.

Multipole radiation

Words: 698 Articles: 12
Radiation zone OurBigBook.com
Multipole radiation expands radiation from localized time-dependent sources into electric and magnetic multipoles. Electric dipole radiation is the leading electric term, while magnetic dipole radiation and higher electric multipoles contribute when the leading term vanishes or higher precision is needed.

Erad​=4πRμ0​​R×(R×p¨​(t−R/c)),Brad​=c1​R×Erad​.
(53)
Their total instantaneous power is
P=6πcμ0​​∣p¨​(t−R/c)∣2.
(54)
Fields of a time-dependent electric dipole

Electric dipole radiation OurBigBook.com
With all electric dipole moments and time derivatives evaluated at t0​=t−r/c, the retarded potentials of a point electric dipole give, for r>0,
E=4πϵ0​1​[r33n(n⋅p)−p​+cr23n(n⋅p′)−p′​+c2rn(n⋅p′′)−p′′​],B=4πμ0​​(r2p′​+crp′′​)×n.
(55)
For a short verification, apply ∇t0​=−n/c and ∂i​nj​=(δij​−ni​nj​)/r when computing E=−∇ϕ−∂t​A and B=∇×A. This produces the displayed r−3, r−2 and r−1 terms. The radiation electric field is transverse and obeys Brad​=n×Erad​/c. The vector triple product then gives the leading Poynting vector n[∣p′′∣2−(n⋅p′′)2]/(16π2ϵ0​c3r2), displaying the angular distribution of electric dipole radiation.

A permanent electric dipole moment of magnitude p0​ rotating perpendicular to a fixed axis emits P=Kω4 in the electric-dipole approximation for radiation, with K=μ0​p02​/(6πc). For fixed mechanical moment of inertia I, weak radiative loss gives Iωω˙=−Kω4 and hence the displayed spin-down law. It assumes ∣ω˙∣≪ω2: the full dipole acceleration has squared magnitude p02​(ω4+ω˙2), whose second term is beyond this leading adiabatic approximation.

Angular distribution of electric dipole radiation OurBigBook.com
The angular distribution of electric dipole radiation measures squared projections of the dipole axis, so a few intensity measurements need not determine that axis or the total radiated power uniquely. For a real unit dipole axis d, the radiation-zone formula is I(n)=3P[1−(d⋅n)2]/(8πR2). Equal intensities along z^, (x^+z^)/2​ and (y^​+z^)/2​ permit four axes, up to reversal:
d ∥ (s1​2​−1, s2​2​−1, 1),s1​,s2​∈{+1,−1}.

Three generally different radiated powers are compatible with the same intensity data. Additional directional measurements or polarization information can remove the ambiguity.

The acceleration covariance in nonrelativistic radiation therefore gives the displayed pattern. Its axial power per solid angle is twice its equatorial value; no observation direction has zero time-averaged power. Integrating gives ⟨P⟩=q2b2ω4/(6πϵ0​c3). The condition bω≪c is essential: relativistic synchrotron radiation has a different beamed pattern.

Magnetic dipole radiation OurBigBook.com
Let a conducting loop of area A rotate about z with normal (cosωt,sinωt,0) in a fixed field Bx. Neglect inductance so I=(BAω/R)sinωt. Put m0​=BA2ω/R. Its vector magnetic moment is
m=2m0​​[sin(2ωt)x+(1−cos(2ωt))y​].
(62)
The static component does not radiate. The remaining component rotates at twice the mechanical frequency and has ∣m¨∣2=4m02​ω4. Thus P=2μ0​B2A4ω6/(3πc3R2). Treating the same sinusoidal current as a fixed-axis moment underestimates this rotating geometry by a factor of eight. The energy source is mechanical rotation, with additional ohmic dissipation and magnetic braking.
Inductance correction to a rotating-loop radiation estimate
Words: 65
Frequency doubling of an induction-driven rotating loop OurBigBook.com
For constant self-inductance L, the steady induced current satisfies LI˙+RI=BAωsinωt, giving amplitude I0​=BAω/R2+ω2L2​ and phase lag. Multiplication by the rotating loop normal again gives a static moment plus a twice-frequency rotating moment of magnitude AI0​/2, independently of lag. Therefore replace the resistance-only denominator R2 in the radiation power by R2+ω2L2. A wire resistance alone is not sufficient for an exact prediction if inductance is appreciable.

Transverse electromagnetic mode (Ez​=Bz​=0)

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
A transverse electromagnetic mode has both electric field and magnetic field transverse to its propagation axis. An ideal two-conductor guide can support such a mode without a geometric waveguide cutoff frequency; an empty simply connected perfect conductor pipe cannot.

Electric and magnetic pressure cancellation in a matched TEM line (fE​=εaVrms2​/(2d2)=μ0​Irms2​/(2a)=fB​)

Words: 76
Transverse electromagnetic mode OurBigBook.com
In a matched lossless parallel-plate transmission line, a single travelling wave obeys V/I=Z0​=(d/a)μ0​/ε​. The electric attraction per unit length is fE​=εaVrms2​/(2d2); each plate feels the field of the other plate, excluding its self-field. Opposite sheet currents give magnetic repulsion fB​=μ0​Irms2​/(2a). Substituting the travelling-wave impedance proves their equality, so the ideal net transverse electromagnetic force is zero at every phase. A standing wave or independent voltage and current need not have this cancellation.

Cherenkov radiation

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Electromagnetic wave OurBigBook.com
Cherenkov radiation is electromagnetic radiation from a charged particle exceeding the medium's phase velocity: c/n(ω)<v<c. Here n(ω) is the positive refractive index at angular frequency ω. The threshold uses phase velocity, not group velocity.[ref]
The beauty of Cherenkov radiation is that uniform motion can generate a sharply directed electromagnetic wave: the medium's response along successive portions of the track adds with matching wave phase on a cone. The moving electric charge drives the medium's electric polarization; the resulting radiation depends on the collective refractive index. This differs from luminescence, where excitation of material is followed by light emission. Both mechanisms can contribute to the same irradiated sample. A visible blue glow alone therefore identifies neither Cherenkov radiation nor a particular radioactive source.
The Cherenkov cone angle turns a measured direction into a constraint on particle speed when the refractive index is known. The Frank-Tamm formula instead predicts the number of emitted photons in a specified wavelength interval. These are complementary observables: the finite-band Cherenkov yield model below shows why both depend on optical dispersion and on which wavelengths are collected. This makes Cherenkov radiation useful for particle detectors, with photon production, transport and detection treated separately.

Cherenkov escape condition at a flat dielectric interface (n1​sinθC​≤n2​)

Words: 62
Cherenkov radiation OurBigBook.com
A photon emitted at angle θC​ to a normally incident particle can cross a planar boundary from index n1​ to n2​ only if Snell's law permits a real transmitted angle. Combining cosθC​=1/(n1​β) with that condition gives n12​−β−2≤n22​. Otherwise the photon undergoes total internal reflection. For a relativistic particle in glass of index 1.55 followed by air, the condition fails despite emission inside the glass.

Kinetic-energy threshold for Cherenkov radiation (Kth​=mc2[(1−n−2)−1/2−1])

Words: 47
Cherenkov radiation OurBigBook.com
At a specified frequency with transparent-medium phase index n>1, Cherenkov radiation requires β>1/n. Inserting the threshold speed into relativistic kinetic energy gives Kth​=mc2[(1−n−2)−1/2−1]. Equality is the kinematic limit; the cone angle and emission vanish there. A dispersive material has different thresholds in different spectral intervals. The result uses phase velocity, not group velocity.

Cherenkov mass inference

Words: 33
Cherenkov radiation OurBigBook.com
The cone relation cosθ=1/(nβ) determines speed. Together with a measured kinetic energy T, the rest mass is m=T/[(γ−1)c2]. The inference requires the radiation to be identified as Cherenkov radiation, and the frequency-dependent phase refractive index must be known.

Cherenkov photon-cone and wavefront-cone angles

Words: 77
Cherenkov radiation OurBigBook.com
For a charge moving at v=βc, the Cherenkov radiation photon direction makes angle θC​ to the trajectory with cosθC​=1/(nβ). The full cone of photon directions has opening 2θC​. The corresponding conical wavefront is perpendicular to those directions and has half-angle μ=π/2−θC​, satisfying sinμ=1/(nβ). Therefore a full opening angle α gives n=1/[βcos(α/2)] for the photon-direction cone, but n=1/[βsin(α/2)] for the wavefront cone. These are different geometrical definitions, not competing approximations to the same angle.

Cherenkov luminescence controls in irradiated liquids

Words: 238
Cherenkov radiation OurBigBook.com
In his 1958 lecture, Pavel Cherenkov recalls the 1934 reports by himself and Sergey Vavilov: radium gamma rays illuminated solutions and their solvents. Weak light was compared using dark-adapted human vision and threshold photometry. Heating and added fluorescence quenching agents left the solvent component and its polarization of an electromagnetic wave unchanged; parallel aqueous fluorescent controls visibly quenched. Its electric vibration direction was parallel to the exciting beam, unlike the compared polarized fluorescence. Further experiments attributed the emission to fast electrons produced by Compton scattering, rather than directly to gamma rays. These comparisons supported a mechanism distinct from ordinary luminescence.[ref]
The evidential step is the controlled comparison, rather than the mere presence of light. A weak glow could include fluorescence from impurities; suppressing a known fluorescent control tests whether the intervention actually works. Visual threshold comparisons also require a stable observer and viewing conditions. These early controls do not themselves calibrate absolute photon yield or supply a single-electron angular scan. Its polarization of an electromagnetic wave comparison also does not by itself measure the Cherenkov cone angle of an individual electron.
Ilya Frank and Igor Tamm supplied the theory in 1937; Ilya Frank also investigated nuclear physics experimentally and later directed neutron research.[ref] Sergey Vavilov, an optics and luminescence researcher and collaborator in the discovery, died in 1951. The 1958 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Pavel Cherenkov, Ilya Frank and Igor Tamm; Sergey Vavilov was not a recipient.[ref]

Cherenkov cone angle (cosθ=1/[βn(ω)])

Words: 337
Cherenkov radiation OurBigBook.com
Let a charged particle travel along +z at constant speed v=βc, with 0<β<1. For a plane electromagnetic wave with wave phase k⋅r−ωt, two points along the track separated by time Δt contribute with phase difference
Δϕ=(kvcosθ−ω)Δt,k=cn(ω)ω​.
(64)
Here θ is the angle between the wave's wave vector and the forward particle track. Constructive addition along a long uniform track requires kvcosθ=ω. Thus
cosθ=βn(ω)1​,βn(ω)>1.
(65)
A real forward cone with nonzero opening exists only above this threshold. At βn=1 the cone closes and the ideal Frank-Tamm formula gives zero yield. For βn<1 there is no allowed angle, rather than an imaginary observable cone. The requirement is phase matching; substituting the group refractive index would describe a different condition.
There is a second geometric derivation when n is constant. In time Δt, the charge advances OP=vΔt, while an earlier spherical phase front has radius OQ=cΔt/n. Its tangent envelope passes through the current position P. The radius OQ is normal to the envelope, so the right triangle gives cosθ=OQ/OP. Rotating about the track makes a cone. Its surface half-angle η is complementary to the emission angle θ, not equal to it.
In a dispersive medium, apply the phase matching derivation separately at each angular frequency. The circle construction uses one fixed phase speed; it does not determine the envelope of a broadband wave packet. In particular, group velocity controls packet propagation under its usual narrow-band assumptions, and the simple complementary-angle construction need not describe a dispersive pulse front. A finite track also broadens the ideal directional selection: adding contributions over duration T gives a factor proportional to sin(ΔT/2)/Δ, with Δ=kvcosθ−ω, rather than an infinitely sharp direction.

Frank-Tamm formula (d2N/(dxdλ))

Words: 494 Articles: 1
Cherenkov radiation OurBigBook.com
For constant particle speed and electric charge q=ze, in a transparent, linear, nonmagnetic medium with isotropy, the Frank-Tamm formula gives the produced photon density:
dxdλd2N​=λ22παz2​(1−β2n2(λ)1​),βn(λ)>1.
(66)
Set it to zero below threshold. Here e is the positive elementary charge, x is track length, λ=2πc/ω is vacuum wavelength, and α is the fine-structure constant. With SI lengths in metres, the density has units m−2; multiplying by dxdλ gives a dimensionless expected count. The explicit SI convention is
α=4πϵ0​ℏce2​,dxdωd2N​=cαz2​(1−β2n2(ω)1​).
(67)
These conventions agree.[ref]
To check the convention, start from E=ℏω=hc/λ and d2N/(dxdE)=αz2sin2θ/(ℏc). Changing variables uses the positive density Jacobian ∣dE/dλ∣=hc/λ2; since h/ℏ=2π, the coefficient becomes 2παz2. No factor of the material refractive index belongs in this Jacobian: λ is not the in-medium wavelength. Multiplication by ℏω gives the corresponding energy loss density in this SI nonmagnetic convention:
dxdωd2W​=4πϵ0​c2z2e2ω​(1−β2n2(ω)1​).
(68)
For an original constant-index example, stipulate n=1.50, β=0.90, z=1 and α=1/137.036. Integration from 400 to 700nm gives
LN​=2πα(1−1.3521​)(400×10−9m1​−700×10−9m1​)≃2.217×104m−1.
(69)
Thus a stipulated 1cm track produces about 222 photons in this band in the ideal model. This is an emitted count before absorption, collection losses and detector response, not a brightness measurement or a measured water yield.

Finite-band Cherenkov yield model

Words: 282
Frank-Tamm formula OurBigBook.com
Choose an original transparent-band model, defined only for 400≤λ≤700nm:
n(λ)=1.28+0.04(λ500nm​)2.
(70)
This chosen refractive index is not a fit to water, glass or the historical liquids. It decreases from 1.3425 to approximately 1.300408, so the threshold 1/n increases across the band. For β=0.75, solving n(λ∗​)=1/β gives
λ∗​=5001/0.75−1.280.04​​nm≃433.013nm.
(71)
Only 400≤λ<λ∗​ emits. Faster particles with β=0.78 and 0.90 emit throughout this chosen band. The Cherenkov cone angle and the Frank-Tamm formula are both evaluated with the same n(λ).
For a 1cm track the chosen model predicts about 0.589, 27.40 and 142.85 emitted photons for β=0.75, 0.78 and 0.90, respectively. An expected count below one is meaningful over repeated equivalent tracks; it is not a fractional photon observed on one track. The near-threshold example illustrates why extending a constant-index approximation across an entire optical band can give the wrong emitting interval.
Finite bandwidth is essential. The 1/λ2 factor cannot be extrapolated down to arbitrarily small wavelength: the chosen material model stops at its stated band. Real optical dispersion changes the threshold and direction, and appreciable absorption requires a complex material response beyond the simple transparent-medium expression. A detected count must also include transport, collection geometry and the detector's wavelength-dependent response. Even a correct produced spectrum therefore does not, on its own, predict perceived colour or observed glow intensity.
